title: Dialogue-aware pipeline throttler and KV residency policy for mixed prompt/response workloads
creator: Aditi Rao
description:
Summary:
We need a scheduler-level intervention to reduce P95 latency and GPU memory churn for mixed prompt/response workloads (chat, assistant flows) that produce frequent short prompts followed by long responses and vice versa. Existing continuous-batcher heuristics prioritize slot fill rate and average length, which causes KV residency thrashing for dialogues that oscillate between short prompts and long generated continuations. This ticket proposes a Dialogue-aware Pipeline Throttler paired with a per-dialogue KV Residency Policy and GPU slab-tiling allocator to: 1) reduce KV cache churn, 2) improve end-to-end P95/P99 for mixed-length conversations, and 3) avoid fragmentation that forces OOMs during long responses.

Goals (success criteria):
- Reduce generation P95 for mixed prompt/response traces by at least 15% vs baseline continuous-batcher.
- Increase KV cache hit rate for in-progress dialogues by >=25%.
- Limit additional GPU memory overhead to <=6% (metadata + residency bookkeeping).
- No regressions on throughput more than -5% for steady-state long-response workloads.

Background and motivation:
- We observe frequent oscillation in token sequence-length distributions for customer chat workloads (user prompt short -> model long -> user short, etc.).
- Continuous batcher groups by token-length slices but has no per-dialogue residency awareness: KV slabs are frequently evicted between turns, causing cold reloads and extra latency during long generations.
- Fragmentation: transient allocations for metadata and partial KV entries lead to slab fragmentation; long responses then trigger conservative evictions or expensive compaction.

Proposed approach (high-level):
1) Dialogue-aware Pipeline Throttler (DPT): a scheduler component that applies a small, tunable artificial pacing to specific incoming short prompt slots when they will soon transition to a long continuation. Pacing is applied only if the slot is likely to improve coalescing with resident KV or reduce expensive KV reloads. Pacing decisions use a lightweight ML signal (logistic model trained on per-dialogue history) + heuristics (recent response length, user cadence).
2) Per-dialogue KV Residency Policy: maintain a residency window for active dialogues (residency score). Each dialogue gets a residency budget (time and bytes) which prefers keeping KV resident across short turns. Under pressure, eviction uses a tiered policy: (a) idle age + token footprint, (b) predictive residency score, (c) coarse LRU fallback.
3) GPU slab-tiling allocator: pre-split KV region into tiling slabs sized for common prefix/resume patterns (tiny/medium/large). Slab allocation reduces fragmentation and simplifies compaction. Integrate with existing GPU allocator hooks for reclaimed kernel buffers.
4) Integration with batcher: expose residency hints to the continuous batcher so that coalescing favors resident dialogs. Add a short-lived reservation for slots expected to continue (3-6 tokens) to avoid preemptive eviction.

Design doc and artifacts:
- Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Dialog-aware+Throttler+Design  (draft)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/9824 (DPT + residency metadata)
- GPU allocator spike PR (tiling): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/9890
- Benchmark dashboards: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/kv-residency/mixed-chat-experiments

Experiments to date (prototype results):
- Setup: representative mixed chat workload (user prompt median 12 tokens, response median 220 tokens, 30% of turns short-short, 40% short-long).
- Baseline: continuous-batcher w/ default KV eviction and global LRU.
- Prototype run: DPT + residency + slab-tiling enabled in experimental runtime.
- Results (aggregate across 24h):
  - P95 generation latency down 18% (baseline 540ms -> 443ms).
  - Throughput improved 12% measured as tokens/sec due to fewer cold KV loads during large responses.
  - KV hit rate for active dialogues +28% (from 62% to 79%).
  - Observed metadata memory overhead ~4.8% of GPU VRAM (acceptable).
  - Edge case: small increase in P50 for long-only traces (+3%) — acceptable per SLOs.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Added scheduler complexity and small ML signal introduces operational surface (model drift). We'll gate the ML decision behind a fast fallback heuristic and feature-flag per tenant.
- Residency bookkeeping increases memory accounting complexity. Need thorough testing for eviction correctness during node restarts.
- Pacing increases latency for a tiny subset of short prompts (when intentionally slowed). We will only pace when predicted net benefit > threshold; telemetry will track affected requests.

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Spike (done): prototype residency metadata + throttler in simulator, initial slab-tiling allocator prototype. (PRs linked above).
- Phase 1 (current sprint): implement residency metadata in runtime, integrate DPT with continuous-batcher, add feature flag and tenant-level opt-in. Instrument KV hit rate, residency churn, and micro-latencies. (ETA: 2 sprints).
- Phase 2: run controlled canary on 10% of hosted traffic for 2 weeks, gather metrics and adjust thresholds.
- Phase 3: rollout to Dedicated as opt-in; follow with on-prem packaging notes for Private.

Next steps / acceptance criteria:
- Complete code review on PR 9824 and 9890 and address allocator edge cases noted by infra (OOM corner cases).
- Add persistent residency checkpointing for node restart recovery.
- E2E canary shows sustained P95 improvement >=15% and KV hit rate increase >=20%.
- Documentation updated in Runtime-ops runbook and Console alerting for KV-churn anomalies.
